hypotheses.title: Data-quality audit
hypotheses.result: 43.2% of urban BioSamples lack a resolved place; 106,803 have a place and a plausible full date. 180 samples have impossible collection dates and are excluded from temporal tests.
hypotheses.question: How much of the catalog is usable for spatial and temporal inference, and where are the gaps?
caveats: Places under 500 inhabitants, districts and facility names are not resolved by design.
A collection date after the first run release is impossible and is treated as an error.

hypotheses.title: Global blind spots of urban genomic surveillance
hypotheses.result: Concentration index 0.82 (95% CI 0.62–0.91); 224 of 573 cities of ≥1 M people have no urban sample within 50 km.
hypotheses.question: Is urban sequencing coverage geographically unequal relative to where people live?
caveats: Counts only samples with a validated country; ~half the catalog has no resolved place.
Coverage is what is public in INSDC, not what is sequenced; national databases and unreleased surveillance data are invisible here.
City population is the GeoNames place population, not the metropolitan area.

hypotheses.title: Surveillance capacity and economic development
hypotheses.result: A 1% higher GDP per capita goes with 1.27% more urban samples per person (95% CI 0.86–1.69, p=1.7e-09), across 159 countries.
hypotheses.question: Do richer countries contribute more public urban sequencing per person?
caveats: Samples are attributed to the country sampled, not the country of the sequencing centre.
World Bank values are the most recent non-missing year in the fetched window.

hypotheses.title: COVID-19 and the structure of urban sequencing
hypotheses.result: Level change at 2020-03: 30% (p=0.46); trend change -2%/yr (p=0.87). Wastewater share 67% → 84%.
hypotheses.question: Did the pandemic cause a level or trend break in urban sequencing, and shift it toward wastewater?
caveats: Discovery queries exclude SARS-CoV-2 amplicon surveillance by default, so the wastewater surge is under-counted, not over-counted.
Collection dates are submitter-reported; 21% of urban samples have none.
Recent years are right-truncated by release lag; --end limits this.

hypotheses.title: Habitat representation
hypotheses.result: Habitat evenness 0.51; municipal wastewater holds 71% of urban samples. Least-studied: transit, surfaces_infrastructure, built_environment. Habitat mix differs by continent (χ²=277, p=6.1e-39).
hypotheses.question: Are some urban habitats systematically under-sampled, and does the imbalance differ by continent?
caveats: Habitat is the eligibility screen's primary context; multi-habitat samples count once.
Discovery queries define which habitats can enter; habitats without query profiles (e.g. hospitals, food markets) are absent by construction.

hypotheses.title: Metadata completeness
hypotheses.result: Joint Wald tests of the assay terms: has_place (p=5.6e-07), has_coordinates (p=1.8e-10), has_collection_date (p=2.1e-08), has_env_broad_scale (p=3.3e-08)
hypotheses.question: Does metadata completeness vary systematically by assay, region and release period?
caveats: Continent is omitted for place and coordinate outcomes, which define it.
GEE gives population-averaged effects; a BioProject random-effects model would give study-specific ones.

hypotheses.title: Concentration in few centres
hypotheses.result: The top 1% of 1,491 submitting centres (15) hold 43% of urban samples; the top 10 hold 38%.
hypotheses.question: Do relatively few research centres produce most public urban sequencing data?
caveats: center_name is the submitter, not the collecting or funding institution; national archives and sequencing cores submit on behalf of many groups.
Spelling variants of one institution are merged only by case and punctuation.

hypotheses.title: Diffusion of sequencing technologies
hypotheses.result: long_read: 48/66 countries adopted, median lag 3 y; illumina_novaseq: 55/66 countries adopted, median lag 4 y; dnbseq_bgi: 13/66 countries adopted, median lag 0 y
hypotheses.question: Do new sequencing technologies reach countries at different times, and does lag track wealth?
caveats: Adoption is observed only through public urban data; a country may use a platform for clinical or unpublished work earlier.
Release year, not sequencing year, is used (sequencing dates are not reported).

hypotheses.title: Eligibility-screen benchmark
hypotheses.result: Labeling sheet of 500 BioSamples written. Label them (two raters, blind to the tier in labeling_key.tsv) and rerun with --labels.
hypotheses.question: How accurate is the rule-based urban eligibility screen against expert labels?
